title: King’s Commonwealth Fellowship Programme 2027: Fully Funded Undergraduate Fellowships for Students from Small Island Developing States
summary: The King’s Commonwealth Fellowship Programme (KCFP) Undergraduate Fellowships 2027 offer a major opportunity for talented students from eligible Commonwealth Small Island Developing States (SIDS) to pursue undergraduate degrees in their home country or immediate region. The programme is designed to strengthen local skills, professional capacity and leadership in countries that face significant development challenges, including the growing effects of climate change. Through financial support, professional development and access to an alumni network, the fellowship seeks to equip young people with the knowledge and skills needed to contribute to the long-term development and resilience of their communities. The 2027 undergraduate fellowship pathway supports students in selected fields including education, engineering, health, environmental health, public health, mathematics education, nursing, sustainable tourism, travel and tourism management, occupational safety and health, geomatics, town and country planning and related disciplines . Applications opened on 14 September 2026 and will close on 14 October 2026 at 15:00 UTC+1 . About the King’s Commonwealth Fellowship Programme Commonwealth Small Island Developing States are particularly exposed to climate-related challenges and face increasing demand for qualified professionals in sectors that are important for national development. The KCFP Undergraduate Fellowships respond to this need by supporting talented students to study at approved KCFP Host Universities located in their home country or, where no approved host university exists in their home country, within their immediate region. Rather than requiring students to relocate to distant countries for their undergraduate education, the programme is structured around developing skills and expertise within participating island communities. The programme particularly seeks to contribute to: Strengthening local professional capacity. Addressing medium-term skills shortages. Improving essential services. Supporting sustainable development. Building community resilience. Developing future professionals and leaders. Creating opportunities for young people to contribute to the long-term prosperity of their countries. The programme also recognises the importance of developing professionals in areas such as education, engineering, health and sustainable tourism. What Does the KCFP Undergraduate Fellowship Cover? Successful fellows receive a package of financial support designed to reduce the major costs associated with undergraduate study. The fellowship provides: 1. Full Tuition Fees The programme covers full tuition fees where full tuition fees are not already covered by the government . This can substantially reduce the financial burden associated with completing an undergraduate degree. 2. Stipend for Basic Living Costs Fellows receive a stipend to cover basic living costs during their studies. This support is intended to help students meet essential day-to-day expenses while undertaking their undergraduate programme. 3. Return Travel to the Home Island Where applicable, fellows receive one return ticket to their home island for every year of study . This provision is particularly relevant to students undertaking their studies outside their home island but within the approved regional arrangement. 4. Professional Development and Alumni Network Beyond financial assistance, the programme is designed to provide fellows with professional development opportunities and access to a strong alumni network. This broader support is intended to help fellows develop careers that serve their communities and contribute to sustainable national development. Who Can Apply for the KCFP Undergraduate Fellowship? The eligibility requirements are specific. Applicants must satisfy all of the conditions established by the programme. To qualify, an applicant must: Hold citizenship or recognised refugee status in one of the eligible Commonwealth Small Island Developing States. Be due to commence undergraduate study between January and December 2027 . Not already hold a higher education qualification, including a bachelor s degree or postgraduate qualification. Select an undergraduate programme from the approved programmes available at the applicant s chosen KCFP Host University. Undertake the programme at an approved KCFP Host University in their home country or, where there is no host university in their home country, at an approved university within their immediate region. Applicants should therefore not assume that any undergraduate course or university will qualify. The programme has published specific host universities and approved undergraduate programmes, and applications for programmes outside the published list will not be considered. Eligible Commonwealth Small Island Developing States The fellowship is specifically intended for applicants from 24 eligible Commonwealth Small Island Developing States across the Caribbean and Americas, Indian Ocean and Pacific regions. Caribbean and Americas Eligible countries listed by the programme are: Antigua and Barbuda Bahamas Barbados Belize Dominica Grenada Guyana Jamaica St Kitts and Nevis St Lucia St Vincent and the Grenadines Trinidad and Tobago Indian Ocean The eligible Indian Ocean SIDS are: Maldives Mauritius Seychelles Pacific The eligible Pacific SIDS are: Fiji Kiribati Nauru Papua New Guinea Samoa Solomon Islands Tonga Tuvalu Vanuatu The programme s eligibility requirements expressly refer to citizenship or refugee status in these Commonwealth SIDS. Approved Host Universities and Undergraduate Programmes One of the most important features of the KCFP Undergraduate Fellowship is that applicants must choose from the approved programmes at participating host universities. The available programmes cover a range of disciplines connected to national development, health, education, engineering, environmental sustainability and tourism. Fiji National University Approved programmes include: Bachelor of Environmental Health Bachelor of Public Health Bachelor of Education (Secondary) (Mathematics Physics) – Mathematics Specialisation Bachelor of Education (Secondary) (Mathematics Physics) – Physics Specialisation Bachelor of Education (Primary) – Primary School Teaching Specialist Applicants from Fiji, Kiribati, Nauru, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu may be considered for the listed programmes at Fiji National University. National University of Samoa Available undergraduate programmes include: Bachelor of Education (Primary) Bachelor of Nursing Bachelor of Health Sciences Bachelor of Science (Secondary Teaching) The listed eligible applicants are from Kiribati, Nauru, Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu . Papua New Guinea University of Technology The approved programmes include: Bachelor of Mechanical Engineering (Honours) Bachelor of Electrical Engineering (Honours) Bachelor of Civil Engineering (Honours) Applicants from Papua New Guinea and Solomon Islands are listed for these programmes. University of Belize The available programmes are: Bachelor in Nursing Bachelor in Mathematics Education Applicants from Bahamas, Belize and Jamaica are listed for these programmes. University of Mauritius The approved programmes include: BEng (Hons) Civil Engineering BSc (Hons) Geomatics BSc (Hons) Town and Country Planning The listed applicants are from Mauritius and Seychelles . University of Technology, Mauritius Students can apply for: BSc (Hons) Occupational Safety and Health Management BSc (Hons) Travel and Tourism Management The programme lists Mauritius and Seychelles as the eligible applicant countries for these programmes. University of the West Indies, Cave Hill The approved programme is: Bachelor of Health Sciences Applicants listed for this programme are from Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Dominica, Grenada, Guyana, Jamaica, St Kitts and Nevis, St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines, and Trinidad and Tobago . Villa College Approved programmes include: Bachelor of Nursing Bachelor of Teaching in Primary and Special Educational Needs Bachelor of Mechanical Engineering (Honours) Bachelor of Electrical and Electronics Engineering (Honours) Bachelor of Civil Engineering (Honours) The listed eligible applicants are from Maldives . How the Host University Arrangement Works The fellowship is designed to allow applicants to undertake their undergraduate studies as close as possible to their home communities. Applicants are expected to study at an approved KCFP Host University located in their home country . If an applicant s home country does not have an approved host university, the applicant may study at another approved KCFP Host University located within their immediate region . This regional approach allows the programme to provide access to approved higher education opportunities while maintaining a strong connection between fellows and their island communities. Applicants should consult the programme s official application guidance because admission requirements can differ according to the undergraduate programme and host university. How Many Fellowships Are Available? A total of 11 King s Commonwealth Fellowships are available through this undergraduate pathway. The fellowships are divided into two groups: Seven fellowships are ringfenced for applicants who are citizens of, or hold recognised refugee status in, seven specified SIDS. Four fellowships are open to applicants from all 24 eligible Commonwealth Small Island Developing States. The seven countries with ringfenced fellowships are: Dominica Grenada Kiribati Nauru Samoa Tonga Tuvalu Applicants from these seven countries will be considered for both the ringfenced fellowships and the wider open competition, provided that they meet all other eligibility requirements. Encouragement for Indigenous Communities The programme states that people belonging to indigenous communities are especially encouraged to apply . However, belonging to an indigenous community is not an eligibility requirement . Applicants who do not belong to an indigenous community can still be eligible if they satisfy the programme s other requirements. When Will the Fellowship Take Place? Successful applicants are expected to commence their undergraduate studies between January and December 2027 . This means prospective applicants should make sure that their selected programme and expected admission timeline align with the 2027 commencement requirement. Application Deadline The King s Commonwealth Fellowship Programme Undergraduate Fellowship application deadline is 14 October 2026 at 15:00 UTC+1 . Applications opened on 14 September 2026 . Applicants should not wait until the final hours to submit their applications. The ACU specifically advises prospective applicants to read the application guidance and frequently asked questions carefully before beginning the application. How to Apply Interested applicants should first establish that they meet all eligibility requirements and that their preferred undergraduate programme appears on the approved programme list. The recommended process is: Check your country eligibility. Confirm that you are a citizen or recognised refugee in one of the 24 eligible Commonwealth SIDS. Confirm your undergraduate status. Applicants must be preparing to commence undergraduate study between January and December 2027 and must not already hold a higher education qualification. Review the approved programmes. Make sure your intended degree is among the programmes approved under the KCFP Undergraduate Fellowship pathway. Check the appropriate host university. Determine which KCFP Host University and programme correspond to your country. Review admission requirements. The programme notes that admission requirements for individual undergraduate programmes are provided in the official application guidance. Read the application guidance and FAQs. The ACU strongly recommends that applicants familiarise themselves with these documents before starting the application. Submit the application before the deadline. Applications must be submitted by 14 October 2026 at 15:00 UTC+1 . The official application page is provided by the Association of Commonwealth Universities. Click HERE to Apply Important Considerations Before Applying The KCFP Undergraduate Fellowship is not an unrestricted undergraduate scholarship. There are several conditions applicants should pay particular attention to. First, applicants must come from an eligible Commonwealth Small Island Developing State. Second, they must not already hold a higher education qualification. Third, the programme of study must be among the approved undergraduate programmes. Applicants should therefore avoid selecting a course simply because it is available at one of the participating universities. The course must specifically appear within the KCFP-approved programme list. Applicants should also verify the admission requirements for their chosen programme because meeting the fellowship eligibility criteria does not necessarily mean that an applicant automatically meets every admission requirement of the host university or degree programme. Why the Programme Matters The KCFP Undergraduate Fellowship is structured around a broader development objective rather than undergraduate education alone. The programme recognises that many Small Island Developing States require additional skilled professionals in areas directly connected to national development and resilience. By supporting students in fields such as: Education Nursing Public health Environmental health Engineering Mathematics education Geomatics Town and country planning Occupational safety and health Travel and tourism the programme seeks to contribute to local capacity and help participating countries respond to long-term development needs. The fellowship therefore combines educational opportunity with an emphasis on developing professionals who can contribute to their communities after completing their studies. Frequently Asked Questions Is the KCFP Undergraduate Fellowship fully funded? The programme provides full tuition fees where full tuition fees are not covered by the government, a stipend for basic living costs and, where applicable, one return ticket to the home island for every year of study. Who is eligible? The fellowship is for eligible citizens or recognised refugees from 24 Commonwealth Small Island Developing States who satisfy the programme s undergraduate study, qualification and approved-programme requirements. Can someone who already has a bachelor s degree apply? No. The programme states that applicants must not hold a higher education qualification, including a bachelor s degree or postgraduate qualification. When must successful applicants begin their undergraduate studies? Applicants must be due to commence undergraduate study between January and December 2027 . Can applicants choose any university? No. Applicants must select an approved undergraduate programme at a KCFP Host University. Where there is no approved host university in the applicant s home country, study may take place at an approved host university within the applicant s immediate region. How many fellowships are available? There are 11 fellowships under this undergraduate pathway: seven ringfenced for applicants from seven specified SIDS and four open to applicants from all 24 eligible Commonwealth SIDS. Are indigenous applicants required to apply? No. The programme particularly encourages people from indigenous communities to apply, but indigenous identity is not an eligibility requirement. What is the application deadline? The deadline is 14 October 2026 at 15:00 UTC+1 . Learn More HERE Conclusion The King s Commonwealth Fellowship Programme Undergraduate Fellowships 2027 provide an opportunity for eligible students from Commonwealth Small Island Developing States to pursue selected undergraduate degrees while receiving substantial financial support. With support covering tuition where applicable, a living-cost stipend and return travel where applicable, the programme is designed not only to support individual students but also to strengthen professional capacity in participating island communities. Because the fellowship is limited to specific countries, approved host universities and approved undergraduate programmes, prospective applicants should carefully check the official eligibility requirements before applying. They should also review the programme-specific admission requirements, application guidance and FAQs well before the deadline. Eligible applicants who intend to begin an approved undergraduate programme in 2027 should take note of the 14 October 2026, 15:00 UTC+1 deadline and complete their applications in accordance with the official instructions. Official application: https://crm.acu.ac.uk/form/kcfp-undergraduate-applications Application guidance and FAQs: Applicants are advised by the ACU to review the Official Guidance and FAQs before beginning their application. title: University of Sheffield AHRC Doctoral Landscape Award 2027/28: Four Fully Funded PhD Studentships in Arts, Humanities and Law
summary: Applications are open for the University of Sheffield AHRC Doctoral Landscape Award (DLA) for 2027/28 entry , offering four fully funded PhD studentships for doctoral researchers undertaking eligible projects within the University’s Faculty of Arts and Humanities. The programme is supported through the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) and forms part of the AHRC North/Northwest Hub , connecting Sheffield’s doctoral researchers with a wider regional network of universities and postgraduate researchers. The award is particularly significant because it is not restricted to traditionally defined arts and humanities disciplines. Eligible applicants may pursue doctoral research through four Sheffield schools, including the School of Law , opening the competition to suitable legal research projects alongside work in English, history, philosophy, digital humanities, languages, arts and societies. Each studentship provides 3.5 years of funding for full-time study , with funding provided pro rata for part-time candidates. The package consists of a maintenance stipend at the UKRI rate — currently £21,805 for the 2026/27 academic year — plus payment of tuition fees at the applicable Home or International rate . International applicants are welcome. However, candidates applying from overseas should note an important limitation: up to one of the four annual studentships may be allocated to an outstanding international candidate , making the international competition particularly selective. Applicants must also pay close attention to the programme’s two-stage application process and two separate deadlines . Candidates first need to submit an application for a PhD place at the University of Sheffield by 14 December 2026 . After obtaining their University study application number, they must separately submit the AHRC DLA funding application by 5:00 PM GMT on 19 February 2027 . Importantly, the published instructions require candidates to submit their PhD application first and obtain an application number before completing the funding form. They do not state that applicants must wait until they have received a formal PhD offer before submitting the scholarship application. The scheme is not open to candidates who are already enrolled on a PhD . Official AHRC Doctoral Landscape Award page at the University of Sheffield About the AHRC Doctoral Landscape Award at the University of Sheffield The AHRC Doctoral Landscape Award , commonly abbreviated to DLA, supports postgraduate researchers working across the arts and humanities. The University of Sheffield has received a Doctoral Landscape Award to support doctoral researchers within its Faculty of Arts and Humanities . Sheffield’s studentships are associated with the AHRC North/Northwest Hub , in collaboration with nine other universities in the region. The structure is intended to provide doctoral researchers with more than individual supervision and financial support. Successful candidates become members of a broader doctoral cohort and are expected to participate actively in: Cohort training Professional development Research activities Interdisciplinary engagement Other activities organized through the DLA North/Northwest Hub Recipients should therefore view the studentship as both PhD funding and participation in a wider doctoral training community. How Many AHRC DLA Studentships Are Available? The University of Sheffield will support: Four full PhD studentships per year. This means that the funding competition is likely to be highly selective. The four awards are available across the Faculty of Arts and Humanities rather than being separately guaranteed to each School. Applicants will initially be assessed within the relevant academic School before shortlisted candidates progress to the Faculty-level selection process. Which University of Sheffield Schools Are Included? The Faculty of Arts and Humanities includes four participating academic Schools: School of English Research undertaken through the School of English may fall within fields such as literature, language, creative writing and related interdisciplinary areas, depending on available supervision and PhD admission requirements. School of History, Philosophy and Digital Humanities This School brings together doctoral research across historical, philosophical and digital-humanities approaches. School of Languages, Arts and Societies Researchers working across languages, cultures, societies and arts-related fields may be based within this School. School of Law Importantly, the School of Law is explicitly included in the Faculty for the purposes of this DLA competition . This means candidates pursuing qualifying arts-and-humanities-oriented doctoral research in law may also apply, subject to obtaining admission to an appropriate Sheffield PhD programme and meeting the funding competition requirements. The inclusion of Law makes this opportunity particularly relevant to prospective PhD researchers working on areas such as legal history, jurisprudence, socio-legal research and other projects that fit the AHRC and Faculty research environment. A Large Arts, Humanities and Law Research Community The University states that the Faculty is home to more than 200 PhD researchers undertaking disciplinary and interdisciplinary research. It also has more than two dozen Faculty Research Centres bringing together: Academic staff Postgraduate researchers Early-career researchers Regional stakeholders This research-centre structure is especially important for applicants because the DLA funding application asks candidates to explain how their proposed research will align not only with their prospective supervisor and School, but also with one or more of the Faculty’s research centres . Candidates should therefore research Sheffield’s institutional environment carefully before submitting their application. Simply demonstrating that a supervisor works on a similar topic may not be sufficient for a strong funding application. Applicants are expected to show how their project fits into the wider intellectual environment available at Sheffield. AHRC DLA Funding Package The studentships are funded for: 3.5 years for full-time study with funding adjusted pro rata for part-time study. The award consists of two major components. 1. UKRI Maintenance Stipend Successful candidates will receive a maintenance stipend at the UKRI rate . The University currently lists the stipend as: £21,805 for the 2026/27 academic year. Candidates entering in 2027/28 should understand that this is the current published rate , rather than assume £21,805 will necessarily remain the exact figure throughout their award. UKRI stipend rates can change between academic years. The maintenance stipend is intended to help doctoral researchers meet living expenses while completing their PhD. 2. Tuition Fee Funding The studentship also includes payment of: Tuition fees at the applicable Home or International rate. This is particularly important for international candidates because overseas PhD tuition fees can be substantially higher than Home fees. The University explicitly states that the award covers: Home tuition fees, where applicable; or International tuition fees, where applicable. Therefore, an international candidate who receives one of these studentships would have the applicable international tuition fees covered under the award. Is the AHRC DLA Open to International Students? Yes. Overseas students are welcome to apply. However, international applicants should understand the funding allocation carefully. The University states that: Up to one of the four studentships may be allocated to an outstanding international candidate. This means international candidates are eligible, but the number of awards potentially available to them is more restricted. The University itself warns that competition for the international place is therefore expected to be particularly intense. Prospective overseas applicants should not interpret international eligibility as meaning there are four international awards. There are four studentships overall, and up to one may go to an outstanding international applicant . Can Current PhD Students Apply? No. The University explicitly states: The scheme is not open to candidates who are already enrolled on a PhD. This is an important eligibility condition. The competition is therefore intended for candidates applying to begin a new PhD programme at Sheffield for the relevant entry cycle rather than current Sheffield PhD students seeking funding partway through an existing doctorate. Two Separate Applications Are Required One of the most important aspects of the AHRC DLA competition is that applying for PhD admission and applying for funding are two separate processes . Candidates cannot simply submit the funding form without first applying for doctoral study. The sequence is: Submit a University of Sheffield PhD study application. Receive your University application number. Submit the separate AHRC DLA funding application using that number. Applicants should therefore begin preparing much earlier than the February scholarship deadline. Step 1: Apply for a PhD Place at the University of Sheffield Candidates must first submit their application for doctoral study through the University of Sheffield’s postgraduate application system. The deadline for the PhD study application is: Monday, 14 December 2026. Submit a University of Sheffield postgraduate research application This first deadline is extremely important. A prospective candidate cannot simply wait until February to begin the process because the funding application requires the study-application number generated following submission of the PhD application. Do You Need a PhD Offer Before Applying for the Scholarship? The published instructions make an important distinction. Candidates must submit their PhD study application first , but the funding instructions do not say that they need to wait for a formal offer of admission. Instead, after submitting the study application, candidates receive an application number . The DLA funding form asks applicants to enter this number. The application guidance identifies it as the nine-digit application number assigned following submission of the University study application . Therefore, the correct sequence is: PhD application submitted → application number received → DLA funding application submitted. Applicants should not unnecessarily delay their funding application while waiting for a formal admission decision unless Sheffield separately instructs them to do so. Step 2: Submit the AHRC DLA Funding Application Once the doctoral application has been submitted and the candidate has received their study application number, they can complete the separate DLA funding form. The final deadline for this stage is: 5:00 PM GMT on Friday, 19 February 2027. AHRC DLA 2027/28 funding application form The University states that the funding application must be completed in one sitting . This makes advance preparation especially important. Use the Application Guidance Template Before Opening the Final Form The University provides an application guidance template that prospective candidates can use to draft their answers before entering them into the final online form. The guidance clearly states that it is not itself the application form . Candidates can use it to prepare responses in advance and then transfer their final answers into the funding form. AHRC DLA 2027/28 application guidance template This is particularly useful because several sections have strict word limits. What Does the AHRC DLA Funding Application Ask For? The 2027/28 application guidance provides considerably more detail about what candidates need to prepare. Applicant Details Applicants are asked to provide basic information including: Forename Surname School to which they have applied Nine-digit PhD application number Email address Candidates select from the participating Schools: School of English School of History, Philosophy and Digital Humanities School of Languages, Arts and Societies School of Law Research Project Proposal The proposed PhD project is central to the funding application. Candidates must provide: Prospective supervisor Applicants should identify the academic they expect to supervise their doctoral research. This reinforces the importance of researching potential supervisors before submitting the application. Project title A clear title for the proposed PhD research is required. 150-word project summary Candidates must summarize their proposed doctoral project in: 150 words. This requires a highly concise explanation of: Research problem Central question Approach Contribution Applicants should not treat this section as simply an abbreviated literature review. Its purpose is to communicate the research project clearly and quickly. Detailed Research Proposal: 500–1,000 Words The DLA application also requires a detailed project proposal of: 500–1,000 words, excluding references. The guidance states that this should match the proposal submitted with the candidate’s application for a PhD place. The proposal must address: The questions or hypotheses the research will examine The research methods that will be used The sources or datasets that will be consulted How the project relates to existing research within the discipline The contribution the research is expected to make to the discipline Candidates should respect the word limit carefully. The guidance explicitly warns that the DLA reserves the right to reject responses that are excessively long. Demonstrating Fit With Sheffield Candidates are also asked to explain in detail how their project aligns with: The expertise of their proposed supervisor or supervisors The research culture of the relevant School One or more Faculty Research Centres This is an important part of the competition. A funding proposal should therefore not read like a generic PhD application that could be submitted to any university. Applicants should demonstrate why Sheffield specifically is an appropriate intellectual environment for the project. This may include identifying: Relevant academics Research groups Faculty centres Methodological expertise Interdisciplinary networks Archives or other research resources Fieldwork and Archival Research The form asks applicants to describe any: Fieldwork Archival visits that will be required for the proposed project. Candidates should therefore think through the practical design of their PhD rather than describing only an abstract research question. Where relevant, this section can help demonstrate that the project is feasible within the funded period. Partner Organizations Applicants may also provide details of external partner organizations that will have direct involvement in their research. Examples identified by the guidance include: Heritage organizations Cultural organizations Policy organizations The form asks candidates to explain what role the organization will play, such as: Co-supervision Exhibition opportunities Public engagement Other direct research involvement Organizations that merely provide access to datasets or research materials do not need to be listed in this section. Academic Qualifications Applicants can enter up to three qualifications already completed . These might include: Bachelor’s or equivalent undergraduate degree Master’s or equivalent postgraduate degree Another university or professional qualification relevant to the project For each qualification, applicants are asked for information such as: Institution Country Type of qualification Programme title Completion date Classification, grade or GPA The DLA page itself does not state one universal minimum GPA or degree classification for all applicants. Candidates must therefore also satisfy the admission requirements for the specific Sheffield PhD programme and School to which they are applying. Qualification Currently in Progress Candidates who are still completing a qualification can provide details of one qualification currently in progress . The form asks for: Institution and country Qualification type Programme title Expected completion date This is relevant for applicants currently completing, for example, a Master’s degree before beginning doctoral study. Relevant Work Experience Work experience is an optional section. Applicants can provide up to: Three relevant work experiences. The University asks candidates to include only employment that is directly relevant to the funding application. For each role, applicants may provide: Employer Job title Description of responsibilities Start date End date, where applicable The fact that this section is optional is important: lack of formal professional experience does not automatically make someone ineligible. Publications Publications are also optional . Candidates can list up to: Five publications. Eligible examples include: Academic papers Conference proceedings Professional reports Book chapters Books Papers that have been formally accepted but are not yet published may be listed. However, applicants should not include work that has not yet been accepted for publication . The application guidance also explicitly reassures candidates not to worry if they have no publications, recognizing that publishing expectations differ considerably between academic disciplines. This means applicants should not assume that an extensive publication record is mandatory. Performances, Compositions, Exhibitions and Presentations The application includes another optional section that is particularly relevant to: Creative-practice researchers Applicants with artistic outputs Candidates who have given research presentations Candidates with professional-practice presentations Applicants can provide up to: Five relevant activities. Examples may include: Performances Compositions Exhibitions Presentations Candidates can describe their own contribution and, where appropriate, provide quantitative evidence such as: Visitor numbers Listener figures Views Reviews Awards This reflects the breadth of arts and humanities research and recognizes research excellence beyond conventional journal publications. Competitive Prizes and Awards Applicants may list up to: Two competitive prizes or awards. The guidance asks candidates to include only awards that were competitively awarded and relevant to demonstrating qualities connected to the application. Examples might relate to: Essay writing Dissertation work Performance Research presentations Professional practice Candidates are also asked to identify whether an award was: Departmental Institutional Regional National International This section is optional. Selection Process Once the funding deadline passes, applications move through several stages. First Stage: School-Level Assessment Applications are shared with the relevant School for the first phase of assessment. This means applicants are initially considered in relation to the academic environment in which their proposed PhD would be based. Second Stage: Faculty Nomination Candidates selected by their School are nominated to a Faculty panel . Faculty Panel: March 2027 The Faculty selection panel is expected to convene in: March 2027. The panel will confirm the final studentship selections. Final Results The University aims to notify all applicants of the final outcome by: The end of March 2027. Candidates should therefore expect the full scholarship decision process to continue for several weeks following the February funding deadline. DLA Cohort Participation Successful candidates do not simply receive funding and work independently with their supervisors. Recipients will become part of the: DLA North/North West Hub cohort and are expected to participate fully in: Cohort training Development activities Other Hub programming Applicants should therefore be interested in contributing to a broader doctoral community alongside completing their individual research. Part-Time Applicants The University describes the 3.5-year studentships as being funded pro rata for part-time study . This indicates that part-time doctoral study can be accommodated under the funding structure, subject to the relevant University arrangements and programme requirements. Applicants considering this route should confirm the precise funding duration and study arrangements with Sheffield. Important Deadlines Prospective applicants should keep both deadlines clearly separated: PhD study application deadline: Monday, 14 December 2026 AHRC DLA funding application deadline: Friday, 19 February 2027 at 5:00 PM GMT Missing the December study deadline may prevent a candidate from obtaining the application number required for the funding competition. The February date should therefore never be treated as the only deadline for this opportunity. How to Prepare a Strong Application Because only four studentships are available, candidates should prepare both their PhD application and funding application carefully. 1. Identify the Right Supervisor Early Your proposal must fit the expertise of your prospective supervisor. Candidates should investigate: Academic research profiles Recent publications Research interests Relevant research centres before finalizing their project. 2. Demonstrate Institutional Fit Do not merely explain why your research topic is important. Explain why the project belongs at Sheffield . Connect your proposal directly to: Supervisor expertise School research strengths Faculty Research Centres 3. Make the Research Question Precise A competitive proposal should identify a researchable question rather than simply naming a broad subject. For example, “international human rights law” is a field. A strong PhD proposal would instead identify a specific legal problem, body of evidence, theoretical debate and potential contribution. 4. Explain the Contribution The funding form explicitly asks what contribution the research will make to the discipline. Candidates should therefore distinguish clearly between: What previous scholarship has established What remains unresolved How their research will address that gap Why that contribution matters 5. Take Methodology Seriously The application asks candidates to explain their research methods. The methodology should be directly connected to the research question rather than included as a generic list of techniques. 6. Respect Every Word Limit The project summary is limited to 150 words , while the detailed proposal is 500–1,000 words excluding references . title: The Carter Center Educational Programs 2027: Internships and Graduate Assistantships in Peace, Health and Operations
summary: The Carter Center Educational Programs offer students and recent graduates opportunities to gain practical professional experience while contributing to initiatives focused on peace, health and organizational operations . The programs are designed to help emerging professionals develop career-relevant skills, explore potential career pathways and contribute to the Carter Center’s mission of advancing peace and health around the world. For more than four decades, the Carter Center’s Educational Programs have supported the professional development of thousands of interns and graduate assistants. According to the Center, nearly 4,000 interns and graduate assistants from around the world have participated in its educational programs, gaining experience while contributing to the organization’s work. The current opportunities include internships for undergraduate students, graduate students and recent graduates , as well as funded graduate assistantships for currently enrolled master’s and doctoral students . About The Carter Center Educational Programs The Carter Center is an organization whose work focuses substantially on promoting peace, improving health and addressing global challenges. Its Educational Programs provide students and early-career professionals with opportunities to gain exposure to this work in a professional environment. The programs are intended not only to provide participants with work experience, but also to help develop a new generation of professionals interested in contributing to peace, health and related fields. Participants can potentially gain experience through program areas including: Peace Health Operations Research and program support Professional and organizational activities related to the Center s work The opportunities can therefore be relevant to students and graduates pursuing a wide range of academic and professional interests. 1. The Carter Center Internship Program The Carter Center s internship program provides opportunities for students and recent graduates to develop professional skills, gain practical experience and explore career options connected to their areas of interest. The program is particularly suited to candidates who can demonstrate strong academic performance alongside academic, professional or personal experiences and interests that relate to the Carter Center s programs. Interns are based in Atlanta, United States , making the location an important consideration for prospective applicants. Who Can Apply for the Internship? To qualify for the internship program, applicants must fall into one of the following categories: Undergraduate juniors Undergraduate seniors Graduate students Recent graduates For recent graduates, the applicant must have graduated within the previous 24 months . This means that the program is aimed primarily at students who are relatively advanced in their undergraduate studies, individuals undertaking graduate-level education, and people who have recently completed their degrees. What Makes a Strong Internship Candidate? The Carter Center indicates that strong candidates demonstrate superior academic ability and have relevant academic, professional or personal experience and interests connected to the Center s programs. Applicants can therefore strengthen their applications by clearly demonstrating how their: Academic background Previous professional experience Research interests Volunteer activities Leadership experience Communication skills International or community engagement Career aspirations relate to the work of the Carter Center. Rather than simply presenting academic qualifications, prospective applicants should demonstrate a clear connection between their background and the type of work carried out by the organization. Internship Program Areas The Carter Center identifies three broad areas in which internship opportunities may be available: Peace Internship opportunities connected to the Peace program can be relevant to individuals interested in areas such as international peacebuilding, conflict prevention, diplomacy, human rights, governance and related global affairs.
